chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Musa ibn Bakr, who said:

Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him), meaning the first (Imam Al-Rida), said to me: 'Why do I see you as pale?' So I said to him, 'A chill has struck me.' So he said to me, 'Eat the meat.' So I ate it. Then he saw me after Friday, and I was still in my pale state, so he said to me, 'Did I not order you to eat the meat?' I said, 'I have not eaten anything else since you ordered me.' So he said, 'And how do you eat it?' I said, 'As a stew (thick soup).' So he said, 'No, eat it as Kabab (roast).' So I ate it. Then he sent for me and called me over after Friday, and behold, the blood had returned to my face. So he said to me, 'Now, yes!'

key_terms.جُمْعَةٍ: A Friday (or a period of a few days)
key_terms.طَبِيخاً: Cooked as a stew or thick soup
key_terms.مُصْفَرّاً: Pale or yellowish in complexion, indicating illness or weakness
key_terms.وَكٌ: A chill or cold affecting the body

ai.seo_question: What is the recommended method of cooking meat to treat a chill according to Imam Al-Rida?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the Imam’s attention to practical health (tibb) and the specific culinary methods that affect digestion and vitality in Shia tradition. The correction from stew (which may be heavier or retain more moisture) to Kabab (grilled/drier) underscores the principle that preparation method significantly influences the medicinal efficacy of food. It reflects the broader Islamic medical tradition where dietary prescriptions are tailored not just to ingredients but to their physical state and cooking technique.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, from Muhammad Bin Sinan, from Musa Bin Bakr who said,

‘Abu Al-Hassan<sup>asws</sup>, meaning the 1st, said to me: ‘What is the matter I<sup>asws</sup> see you as pale?’ So I said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘Pain has struck me’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said to me: ‘Eat the meat’. So I ate it. Then he<sup>asws</sup> saw me after the Friday, and I was (still) upon my pale state, so he<sup>asws</sup> said to me: ‘Did I<sup>asws</sup> not order you with eating the meat?’ I said, ‘I have not eaten anything else since you<sup>asws</sup> ordered me’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘And how did you eat it?’ I said, ‘Cooked’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘No, eat it as Kabab (roast)’. So I ate it. Then he<sup>asws</sup> sent a message to me, so he<sup>asws</sup> called me over after Friday, and the blood had returned in my face. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Now, yes!’
en.sarwar: 3. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Isa from Muhammad ibn Sinan from Musa ibn Bakr who has said the following:

“Once abu al-Hassan, al- Awwal asked me, ‘Why do you look pale?’ I replied, ‘I suffer from a certain pain.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘Eat meat.’ I ate meat and the next Friday he (the Imam) saw me as pale as before and said, ‘Did I not tell you to eat meat?’ I replied, ‘Yes, I have not eaten anything other than meat from the day you instructed me.’ He (the Imam) then asked, ‘How did you eat?’ I replied, ‘I ate as mixed with other items.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘No, eat as kabab.’ I then ate kabab and he (the Imam) sent for me next Friday when my blood level had come back in my face, and he (the Imam) said to me, ‘Now it is good, you are fine.’”
